generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, self-efficacy decides whether you keep going on the parts that feel hard, such as statistics or research design. Believing you can handle a specific task grows as you master small pieces of it. Motivation matters too: a student driven to understand the discipline tends to outlast one driven only by the next mark, especially when the work is demanding.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students face the same demanding task: a statistics assignment neither feels ready for.

Tom is driven mainly by the mark and has little belief in being able to do statistics. The first hard question confirms the fear, and he concludes there is no point and hands in a thin attempt. Low self-belief and a focus on the mark alone made the task easy to abandon.

Amara also finds it hard, but starts by mastering one worked question, then a second, building a sense of being able to do it. She wants to understand the analysis, not just pass, and asks a friend who struggled with it last year how they got through. Belief and learning motivation keep her effort going to the end.

Both students found the task hard. Only Amara built the self-efficacy, and leaned on the motivation, needed to finish it well.
generatedProse.summary: In psychology, what keeps you going on hard work is self-belief and the right kind of motivation. Self-efficacy is your belief that you can do a specific task, such as a statistical analysis, and it grows through mastery, seeing others succeed, feedback and managing stress. Learning motivation sustains effort better than chasing marks alone. You can now tell the two motivations apart and build self-efficacy on purpose. The last lesson turns this into goals.

check.body: In the worked example, how did Amara build self-efficacy for the statistics assignment?

items.text: By mastering one worked question, then another, and asking someone who had struggled through it.
By reminding herself that the mark was all that mattered.
By deciding statistics was simply not for her.
By handing in a thin attempt to get it over with.

feedback.correct: That's right. Mastering small parts and seeing someone like her succeed built Amara's self-efficacy.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the moves that gave Amara a sense of being able to do it.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara built self-efficacy by mastering one question then another, and by asking someone who had struggled through it. The others describe low self-belief.
